attributes.title: Level 10

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you test out the project by moving the Player sprite around the tilemap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the food projectiles overlap each dinosaur sprite?

❓ What might be added to improve the User Experience (UX) of this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to both play the project and review the starter code. Prompt the ninja to notice that there are 2 different dinosaur sprite kinds (Herbivore and Carnivore) that map to different dinosaur images. Ask the ninja to consider what might happen when different food projectiles overlap each sprite kind.

💡 In this activity, the ninja will explore adding the Status Bar and Timer extensions to improve the User Experience (UX). The Status Bar creates a health meter above a sprite, which can be used to inform game play.
steps.instructions:
Begin by exploring the existing project!


Click ▶ to explore the tilemap on screen. Use the direction buttons to move the Player sprite around the screen, then use the A and B buttons to launch food projectiles at the dinosaur sprites.


Notice that nothing happens when the projectiles overlap the dinosaur sprites. This will be addressed with the Status Bar extension. Click Extensions then scroll down to add the status-bar extension to the project.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use let to create the status bar sprite outside of the createStatusBar function, but not inside the function, so that it can be accessed inside other functions in the code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the statusbars.create function do? How might it be used to improve the User Experience (UX) of this project?

❓ Why does the statusbar sprite need to be declared before it is used in the createStatusBar function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The statusbars.create function creates a status bar sprite that represents health meter, and can be updated throughout a project. Other functions are required to attach the status bar to a sprite, set its colors, and set its maximum value. 

💡Point out the ninja that the statusbar sprite will need to be referenced throughout the project. As a result, it needs to be declared outside of the createStatusBar function, in order to be accessed everywhere throughout the code.
steps.instructions:
Create a function that will add a status bar to each dinosaur sprite!


Open Status Bar and drag [create status bar sprite width (20) height (4) kind (kind)] below the code that creates a player and dinosaur sprite under // project initialization. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


let statusbar = statusbars.create(20, 4, StatusBarKind.Health)

The statusbars.create function takes 3 parameters: width, height, and kind. Set the width and height parameters to 0 so the status bar does not appear until it is updated later on in the code. 


Create a new function below the existing functions under // project initialization named createStatusBar that takes 2 parameters: a sprite sprite parameter and a maxValue number parameter. Inside the function definition, add another [create status bar sprite width (20) height (4) kind (kind)] and leave the width and height parameters set to the default arguments. Delete let so that the previously declared status bar is updated.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the createStatusBar function’s parameters to pass arguments to the max and attachToSprite functions?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the status bar’s starting and max values be set to?

❓ What colors might be used to display a sprite’s health on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that in this project, the status bar is assigned a value that sets the starting amount for the health meter (e.g. 0). The max value sets the value that the status bar needs to reach in order to become “full”. In other projects, the status bar value might be set to a larger number that decreases as events occur throughout the game.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider what colors to use in the status bar so that it is clearly visible against the tilemap and the sprite images.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the attachToSprite function is needed in order to display a status bar above a sprite. Without the function, the status bar will appear in the middle of the screen.
steps.instructions:
Customize the appearance of the status bar.


Inside the createStatusBar function definition, type the status bar sprite’s name, a dot operator, and value to set the status bar’s starting value to 0. Type the status bar sprite’s name again, a dot operator, and max to set the status bar’s max value to the maxValue parameter.


Open Status Bar and drag out [set (statusbar) fill to (7) background (2)] to the bottom of the function definition. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

statusbar.setColor(7, 2)

The setColor function can take 3 parameters: fill color, background color, and an optional drain color to show while the value is being changed. Tinker with the 2 color parameters, or leave the default arguments.


Open Status Bar and drag out [attach (statusbar) to (mySprite)] to the bottom of the function definition. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

statusbar.attachToSprite(null) 

The attachToSprite function can take 3 parameters: sprite to follow, padding, and offset. Use the sprite parameter as the parameter for this function.

steps.hints: ❓Did you pass different maxValue arguments to the createStatusBar function to determine how many food projectiles will need to overlap each dinosaur sprite kind to fill its status bar?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might each dinosaur sprite kind’s max value be set to? 

❓ What happens when the createStatusBar function is called? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the max value represents the value that the status bar needs to reach in order to become “full”. In this activity, projectiles will be used to increase each status bar’s value. By passing a larger maxValue argument, the Player sprite will need to send additional projectiles toward the dinosaur sprite, in order for it the status bar to reach “full”. 

💡 When the createStatusBar function is called, a status bar will be created and attached to each dinosaur sprite on screen. The status bar will have 2 different colors and have different max values for each sprite kind.
steps.instructions:
Call the createStatusBar function to see the status bars appear above each dinosaur sprite!


Locate the createDinos() function in the code already in the project. Inside the conditional that sets the sprite image and kind, call the createStatusBar function for both sprite kinds, passing the sprite name as the first argument and the number to set as the maxValue as the second argument. Set the maxValue to be different for the Herbivore and Carnivore sprites.


Click ▶ to see a status bar appear above each dinosaur sprite on the tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an addition assignment operator += to add 1 to the status bar’s value?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the getStatusBarAttachedTo function do? Why is it useful? 

❓ Why is it necessary to add a dot operator and value to the getStatusBarAttachedTo function?

❓ What happens when each dinosaur sprite kind is overlapped by the matching food projectile?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The getStatusBarAttachedTo function makes the status bar attached to a specific sprite accessible. This function is needed to add, subtract, or update a specific sprite’s status bar. A dot operator and value must be added to the function in order to identify the current amount (and remaining capacity) of a specific sprite’s status bar.

💡 Now, when each dinosaur sprite kind is overlapped by the correct food projectile, the projectile will be destroyed and the sprite’s status bar value will increase by 1.

💡 Point out to the ninja that they will need to use an addition assignment operator += to add 1 to the status bar’s value, instead of an increment operator ++. The same would be true to decrease the status bar’s value by 1 (-= instead of --).
steps.instructions:
Increase the status bar value when the dinosaur sprite is overlapped by the correct food projectile.


Open Status Bar and drag [status bar kind (kind) attached to (mySprite)] into the conditionals in both onOverlap events. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


statusbars.getStatusBarAttachedTo(

StatusBarKind.Health, null)


The getStatusBarAttachedTo function takes 2 parameters: status bar kind and sprite. Use the default Health kind and update the sprite parameter to otherSprite from the onOverlap event.


Then, type a dot operator and value, then increase the status bar’s value by 1.


Click ▶ to see the status bar’s value increase when the correct food projectile overlaps a dinosaur sprite.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an equality operator == to check if the value of the status bar is equal to the value assigned as the max of the status bar?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when a sprite’s status bar becomes full?

❓ What number should be used inside the conditionals in each onOverlap event? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When a sprite’s status bar becomes full, the dinoFull function will be called, which turns the sprite’s GhostThroughSprites flag on, adds 1 to the dinoCount, and runs a sprite effect.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the number argument passed to the maxValue parameter should be used in each conditional, not the variable name.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the status bar reaches its max value!


Inside both onOverlap events, add a second conditional that checks if the getStatusBarAttachedTo function’s value is equal to the number passed as the maxValue to the function that created the status bar. 


Call the dinoFull function inside the conditional, passing the otherSprite parameter to that function to set a GhostThroughSprites sprite flag and to start a sprite effect on that sprite to let the player know the dinosaur’s status bar is now full.


Click ▶ to test what happens when the dinosaur sprite’s status bar reaches its max value.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use convertToText to change the dinoCount number value to a string?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What colors might be used for the text sprite’s foreground and background? 

❓ What type of value can be passed to the setText function? 

❓ What values might be used to set the text sprite’s font size, icon, border, and position? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the score text sprite will be a fixed image that appears in the screen’s corner. This is a User Interface (UI) feature that will inform the user of how many dinosaur status bars have been filled throughout the game. The ninja should select strategic colors and values to customize the text sprite’s appearance so that it is clearly visible on screen and communicates its purpose to the user.

💡 Remind the ninja that the setText function can only accept string values. As a result, the convertToText function is needed in order to change the dinoCount number value to a string.
steps.instructions:
Count the number of dinosaurs fed!


Notice the Text Sprite extension has already been added to the project. Open Text Sprite and drag [text sprite (text)] under // project initialization. Name the text sprite score then set it to an empty string "" and choose the text and background colors.


Create a createScore function to organize the text sprite’s code. Inside the function definition, use the setText function to set the text sprite to display the dinoCount variable already in the code. Then use the setMaxFontHeight, setIcon, and setBorder functions to customize the text sprite. 


Position the text sprite in the upper right or left corner of the screen. Pin the text sprite in that location, even as the camera moves, using the setFlag function with the RelativeToCamera sprite flag set to true.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use convertToText to change the updated dinoCount number value to a string?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the callScene function is called if sceneNum is equal to 2?

❓ What happens when the dinoFull function is called? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If sceneNum is equal to 2 when the callScene function is called, the game level will be set and the score variable will be displayed on screen.

💡 When the dinoFull function is called, the dinosaur sprite’s GhostThroughSprites flag will be turned on, a sprite effect will run, 1 will be added to the dinoCount, and the dinoCount will be updated on screen.

💡 Remind the ninja that the setText function can only accept string values. As a result, the convertToText function is needed in order to change the dinoCount number value to a string.
steps.instructions:
Display and update how many dinosaurs are fed on screen.


Call the createScore function inside the callScene function definition as part of the conditional that checks for sceneNum 2. 


Use a setText function to update the text sprite inside the dinoFull function every time the dinoCount variable increases.


Click ▶ to view the text sprite on screen, then tinker with the text sprite functions to adjust the appearance, as needed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you place the projectile code inside the brackets of the throttle function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the throttle function do? How might it be useful in a project? 

❓ What might the timer parameter be set to in the throttle function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The Timer extension can be used to delay actions from happening until a certain amount of time has passed. It might be used to delay how frequently sprites appear on screen, showing text to the user, or to create sequential events in a project.

💡 The throttle function delays a repeated action in a game, until a certain amount of time has passed. In this example, it is used to delay how frequently the Player sprite can send projectiles towards the dinosaur sprites. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to think about what value to use as the time parameter in the function, in order to make the game challenging but not impossible.
steps.instructions:
Control how often the Player sprite can launch a food projectile.


Notice that the Player sprite can “spam press” the A and B buttons to rapidly launch food projectiles. To control this, add a throttle to the sendFood function definition.


Click Extensions then scroll down to add the Timers extension to the project. Open Timer then drag [run code for (action) at most once every (500) do] into the outer if conditional, inside the sendFood function definition, surrounding the existing projectile code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

timer.throttle(“action”, 500, function() {}) 

The throttle function takes 2 parameters: key and time. Leave the default value for the key parameter, but tinker with the time parameter to control how often the user can press the A or B button to launch a projectile.


Click ▶ to test the throttle of the projectiles!

steps.hints: ❓Did you cut and paste all of the code for each text sprite inside the brackets of the after functions to ensure the height, position, and kind code run correctly?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the after function do? How might it be useful in a project? 

❓ What chunk of code should be placed inside each after function?

❓ Why do the setPosition and setKind functions also need to be placed inside each after function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The after function runs a chunk of code after the specified amount of time has passed in the project. This function can be useful for sequencing events in a project, such as displaying different text messages on screen after one another. 

💡 Because the after function has its own set of curly brackets, anything created inside of the block statement cannot be accessed outside of it. In order to set each text sprite’s position and kind, the functions must be placed inside each after function.
steps.instructions:
Sequence the timing of the introduction text!


Notice the text sprites in the createIntroText function do not appear on screen. To fix this, add timer code to the function definition so each text sprite appears after a set time delay.


Open Timer then drag [run code after (500) do] into the top of the createIntroText function definition. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

timer.after(500, function() {}) 

The after function takes 1 parameter: time. Drag 2 additional after functions into the createIntroText function definition, setting the parameters to 0, 1000, and 2000, respectively. Then, cut and paste the existing text sprite code into the 3 different after functions to sequence the timing of the text appearing on screen. Tinker with which sprites go into which after functions so the text appears on screen in a logical sequence.


Then, add one additional after function that uses 5000 as the parameter to destroy all the Title sprites, change the gameStart variable, and call the next scene to run.


Click ▶ to see the introduction text appear on screen in a timed sequence, before the game starts.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the startCountdown function to a reasonable number of seconds to make the game challenging, but not too hard or too easy?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the countdown be set to so that the game is challenging, but not impossible?

❓ What other User Interface (UI) and User Experience (UX) features might be added to this project? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider the UI/UX features that they’ve seen before and may already be familiar with (such as splash/game over screens, a choice menu, allowing the user to select their character, text that appears when a user interacts with something, etc.). Ask the ninja to consider how adding UI/UX features to a project improves the User Experience (UX) of a game.
steps.instructions:
Complete the game by adding a timer!


Add code to set a countdown timer inside the callScene function definition as part of the conditional that checks for sceneNum 2. 


Then, add a // game over screen comment, and use an onCountdownEnd function underneath to change the gameStart variable to false, add a splash screen that shows the user how many hungry dinosaurs they fed, and reset the game.


Click ▶ to play the completed game, noticing how the Status Bar and Timer extensions enhance the overall game play.

subgroups.title: Feed The Hungry Dinos!
subgroups.introduction: Create project enhancements using the Status Bar and Timer extensions to show a sprite’s health meter and control the timing of actions in a game.

validationItems.text: Create a status bar to add to each dinosaur sprite.
Use a createStatusBar function with sprite and maxValue parameters to customize the appearance of the status bar.
Increase the status bar value when a food projectile overlaps a dinosaur sprite.
Trigger something to happen when the status bar reaches its max value.
Pin a text sprite to the top corner of the screen to show how many dinosaur sprites were fed.
Use throttle to control how often the Player sprite can launch a projectile.
Sequence the timing of on screen text.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 10 of Brown Belt! Before you create your final Brown Belt project, there are a few neat tricks to learn that could take your game to the next level! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 10:

badges.title: Extension Explorer
badges.description: Use the minimap, status bar, timer, and raycasting extensions to enhance a project.

badges.title: Bird’s Eye View
badges.description: Create and pin a minimap displaying a smaller representation of sprites and the tilemap in a corner of the screen.

badges.title: Gauging the Action
badges.description: Make something happen based on the value of a status bar.

badges.title: Wait for the Signal
badges.description: Use throttle to delay an action in a game.

badges.title: Right on Cue
badges.description: Run a chunk of code after a certain amount of time has passed.

badges.title: In-Depth Image
badges.description: Create a 3D version of a tilemap from a sprite’s perspective.

badges.title: Points of View
badges.description: Toggle between 3D and top-down views of a tilemap.
